Cud
KUD
noun
Old English cwidu, that which is chewed; the food a ruminant returns from the first stomach to the mouth to be chewed a second time. Hence to chew the cud, to ruminate, to turn a thing over slowly.

Biblical Definition

The cud is the food a ruminant beast brings up again out of its stomach to chew a second time. With the parted hoof it forms the twofold test of the clean beast in the ceremonial law, and it is the inward mark as the hoof is the outward. “Nevertheless these shall ye not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the hoof: as the camel, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you” (Lev 11:4). Neither mark availed without the other. The whole apparatus had one declared end, and it was not diet but discernment: “Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean… which I have separated from you as unclean” (Lev 20:25). The priests were charged to teach Israel that very habit — “the difference between the holy and profane” (Eze 44:23) — and every meal rehearsed the lesson until it was in the bone. That is what the cud pictures: not a glance at the word but the slow return to it, the second and third chewing, the meditating day and night by which truth is broken down and turned into strength. The ceremony is abolished in Christ; the faculty it trained is commanded still, for strong meat belongs to them “who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil” (Heb 5:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Food returned from the first stomach of a ruminant to be chewed again; hence to ruminate, to meditate.

CUD, the food which ruminating animals return from the first stomach into the mouth to be chewed a second time.

Old English cwidu, that which is chewed; whence to chew the cud, to ruminate.

In the law it is the inward mark of the clean beast (Lev 11:3-4; Deu 14:6).

The camel chews the cud yet is unclean, wanting the parted hoof (Lev 11:4).

Figuratively, to turn a matter over in the mind; to meditate at length.

Key Scripture

Lev 11:4 — "Nevertheless these shall ye not eat of them that chew the cud, or of them that divide the hoof: as the camel, because he cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you."

Lev 20:25 — "Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean, and between unclean fowls and clean: and ye shall not make your souls abominable by beast, or by fowl, or by any manner of living thing that creepeth on the ground, which I have separated from you as unclean."

Eze 44:23 — "And they shall teach my people the difference between the holy and profane, and cause them to discern between the unclean and the clean."

Heb 5:14 — "But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil."

Modern Corruption

An age that skims has lost the chewing of the cud — and a church that will not put difference between the holy and the profane has lost what the law was given to teach.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live loss is a habit, not a doctrine. The clean beast is marked by rumination: it takes the food down, brings it up, and works it a second time until the good of it is extracted. The Christian mind was made for the same labour — the psalmist’s meditation day and night, the Bereans searching daily, the Puritan practice of taking one text into the week and returning to it until it yielded. What has displaced it is the skim: the verse-image, the clip, the plan that measures reading by chapters covered rather than truth digested, the sermon consumed at double speed and forgotten by dinner. A man may read the whole Bible in a year and chew nothing. The remedy is unfashionable and simple — less at one sitting, returned to more often, prayed over, spoken back to God, until the word is not merely swallowed but assimilated and turned into blood and bone.

The second thing to recover is what the two marks together were teaching. The camel ruminates and is unclean; the swine parts the hoof and is unclean; only where the inward and the outward agree is the beast clean. So it is with men. There is a religion of the visible foot — the correct walk, the attended service, the reputation kept — with no meditation behind it; and there is a religion of the ruminating mouth — the man full of doctrine and warm feeling whose tread in the dust betrays him. Neither is cleanness. Christ has abolished the shadow and no Christian is bound to the table of beasts (Col 2:16–17; Act 10:15), but He has not abolished the discernment the shadow trained. Ezekiel’s charge to teach the difference between the holy and the profane now falls on the eldership, and the mark of maturity in Hebrews is precisely a sense exercised by use to tell good from evil. Discrimination is not a vice to repent of; in Scripture it is a sign of growth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The chewed-again food of the ruminant; the inward mark of the clean beast, and Scripture’s picture of meditation.

expand to see more

Cud — Old English cwidu, that which is chewed.

Hebrew gerah, the cud; the clean beast bringeth up and chews again.

It is the inward mark, as the parted hoof is the outward.

The camel chews the cud and is unclean still — one mark never sufficed (Lev 11:4).

Figuratively: meditation, the slow second chewing of the word of God.

Usage

"Chewing the cud is meditation — the truth taken down, brought up, and worked again."

"The camel ruminates and is unclean: inward warmth without an outward walk proves nothing."

"The ceremony is fulfilled in Christ; the discernment it trained is commanded still (Heb 5:14)."
